On the Milnor formula in arbitrary characteristic 00footnotetext: 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 14H20; Secondary 32S05.
Key words and phrases: plane singularity, Milnor number, degree of conductor, factorization of polar curve.
The first-named author was partially supported by the Spanish Project MTM 2016-80659-P.

Evelia R. García Barroso    Arkadiusz Płoski
Abstract

The Milnor formula μ=2​δ−r+1\mu=2\delta-r+1 relates the Milnor number μ\mu, the double point number δ\delta and the number rr of branches of a plane curve singularity. It holds over the fields of characteristic zero. Melle and Wall based on a result by Deligne proved the inequality μ≥2​δ−r+1\mu\geq 2\delta-r+1 in arbitrary characteristic and showed that the equality μ=2​δ−r+1\mu=2\delta-r+1 characterizes the singularities with no wild vanishing cycles. In this note we give an account of results on the Milnor formula in characteristic pp. It holds if the plane singularity is Newton non-degenerate (Boubakri et al. Rev. Mat. Complut. (2010) 25) or if pp is greater than the intersection number of the singularity with its generic polar (Nguyen H.D., Annales de l’Institut Fourier, Tome 66 (5) (2016)). Then we improve our result on the Milnor number of irreducible singularities (Bull. London Math. Soc. 48 (2016)). Our considerations are based on the properties of polars of plane singularities in characteristic pp.

Dedicated to Antonio Campillo on the occasion of his 65th birthday

Introduction

John Milnor proved in his celebrated book [17] the formula

μ=2​δ−r+1,\mu=2\delta-r+1, (M)

where μ\mu is the Milnor number μ\mu, δ\delta the double point number and rr the number of branches of a plane curve singularity. The Milnor’s proof of (M) is based on topological considerations. A proof given by Risler [21] is algebraic and shows that (M) holds in characteristic zero.

On the other hand Melle and Wall based on a resultd by Deligne [5] proved the inequality μ≥2​δ−r+1\mu\geq 2\delta-r+1 in arbitrary characteristic and showed that the Milnor formula holds if and only if the singularity has not wild vanishing cycles [16]. In the sequel we will call a tame singularity any plane curve singularity verifying (M).

Recently some papers on the singularities satisfying (M) in characteristic pp appeared. In [1]) the authors showed that planar Newton non-degenerate singularities are tame. Different notions of non-degeneracy for plane curve singularities are discussed in [10]. In [18] the author proved that if the characteristic pp is greater than the kappa invariant then the singularity is tame. In [7] and [11] the case of irreducible singularities is investigated. Our aim is to give an account of the above-mentioned results.

In Section 1 we prove that any semi-quasihomogeneous singularity is tame. Our proof is different from that given in [1] and can be extended to the case of Kouchnirenko nondegenerate singularities ([1, Theorem 9]). In Section 2 and 3 we generalize Teissier’s lemma ([22, Chap. II, Proposition 1.2]) relating the intersection number of the singularity with its polar and the Minor number to the case of arbitrary characteristic and reprove the result due to H.D. Nguyen [18, Corollary 3.2] in the following form: if p>μ​(f)+ord​(f)−1p>\mu(f)+\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1 then the singularity is tame.

Section 4 is devoted to the strengthened version of our result on the Milnor number of irreducible singularities.

1 Semi-quasihomogeneous singularities

Let 𝐊\mathbf{K} be an algebraically closed field of characteristic p≥0p\geq 0. For any formal power series f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] we denote by ord​(f)\mbox{\rm ord}(f) (resp. in​(f)\mbox{\rm in}(f)) the order (resp. the initial form of ff). A power series l∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]l\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] is called a regular parameter if ord​(l)=1\mbox{\rm ord}(l)=1. A plane curve singularity (in short: a singularity) is a nonzero power series ff of order greater than one. For any power series f,g∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f,g\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] we put i0​(f,g):=dim𝐊𝐊⁡[[x,y]]/(f,g)i_{0}(f,g):=\dim_{\mathbf{K}}\mathbf{K}[[x,y]]/(f,g) and called it the intersection number of ff and gg. The Milnor number of ff is

μ⁡(f):=dim𝐊𝐊⁡[[x,y]]/(∂f∂x,∂f∂y).\mu(f):=\dim_{\mathbf{K}}\mathbf{K}[[x,y]]/\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right).

If Φ\Phi is an automorphism of 𝐊⁡[[x,y]]\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] then μ⁡(f)=μ⁡(Φ⁡(f))\mu(f)=\mu(\Phi(f)) (see [1, p. 62]). If the characteristic of 𝐊\mathbf{K} is p=char​𝐊>0p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}>0 then we can have μ⁡(f)=+∞\mu(f)=+\infty and μ⁡(u​f)<+∞\mu(uf)<+\infty for a unit u∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]u\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] (take f=xp+yp−1f=x^{p}+y^{p-1} and u=1+xu=1+x).

Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced (without multiple factors) power series and consider a regular parameter l∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]l\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]]. Assume that ll does not divide ff. We call the polar of ff with respect to ll the power series

𝒫l​(f)=∂(f,l)∂(x,y)=∂f∂x​∂l∂y−∂f∂y​∂l∂x.{\cal P}_{l}(f)=\frac{\partial(f,l)}{\partial(x,y)}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial l}{\partial x}.

If l=−b​x+a​yl=-bx+ay for (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\neq(0,0) then 𝒫l​(f)=a​∂f∂x+b​∂f∂y{\cal P}_{l}(f)=a\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+b\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}.

For any reduced power series ff we put 𝒪f=𝐊⁡[[x,y]]/(f){\cal O}_{f}=\mathbf{K}[[x,y]]/(f), 𝒪f¯\overline{{\cal O}_{f}} the integral closure of 𝒪f{\cal O}_{f} in the total quotient ring of 𝒪f{\cal O}_{f} and δ⁡(f)=dim𝐊𝒪f¯/𝒪f\delta(f)=\dim_{\mathbf{K}}\overline{{\cal O}_{f}}/{\cal O}_{f} (the double point number). Let 𝒞{\cal C} be the conductor of 𝒪f{\cal O}_{f}, that is the largest ideal in 𝒪f{\cal O}_{f} which remains an ideal in 𝒪f¯\overline{{\cal O}_{f}}. We define c(f)=dim𝐊𝒪¯{/𝒞c(f)=\dim_{\mathbf{K}}\overline{\cal O}_{f}/{\cal C} (the degree of conductor) and r⁡(f)r(f) the number of irreducible factors of ff. The semigroup Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) associated with the irreducible power series ff is defined as the set of intersection numbers i0​(f,h)i_{0}(f,h), where hh runs over power series such that h≢0h\not\equiv 0 (mod​f\mathrm{mod}\,f).

The degree of conductor c⁡(f)c(f) is equal to the smallest element cc of Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) such that c+N∈Γ⁡(f)c+N\in\Gamma(f) for all integers N≥0N\geq 0 (see [2], [9]).

For any reduced power series ff we define

μ¯​(f):=c⁡(f)−r⁡(f)+1.\overline{\mu}(f):=c(f)-r(f)+1.

In particular, if ff is irreducible then μ¯​(f)=c​(f)\overline{\mu}(f)=c(f).

Proposition 1.1

Let f=f1⋯fr∈𝐊[[x,y]]f=f_{1}\cdots f_{r}\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series, where fif_{i} is irreducible for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Then

  1. (i)

    μ¯​(f)=μ¯​(u​f)\overline{\mu}(f)=\overline{\mu}(uf) for any unit uu of 𝐊⁡[[x,y]]\mathbf{K}[[x,y]].

  2. (ii)
    μ¯​(f)+r−1=∑i=1rμ¯​(fi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤ri0​(fi,fj).\overline{\mu}(f)+r-1=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\overline{\mu}(f_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j}).
  3. (iii)

    Let ll be a regular parameter such that i0​(fi,l)≢0i_{0}(f_{i},l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Then

    i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ¯​(f)+i0​(f,l)−1.i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\overline{\mu}(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.
  4. (iv)

    μ¯​(f)=μ​(f)\overline{\mu}(f)=\mu(f) if and only if μ⁡(f)=2​δ​(f)−r⁡(f)+1\mu(f)=2\delta(f)-r(f)+1.

  5. (v)

    μ¯​(f)≥0\overline{\mu}(f)\geq 0 and μ¯​(f)=0\overline{\mu}(f)=0 if and only if ord​(f)=1\mbox{\rm ord}(f)=1.

Proof. Property (i)(i) is obvious. To check (i​i)(ii) observe that

∑i=1rμ¯​(fi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤ri0​(fi,fj)=∑i=1rc⁡(fi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤ri0​(fi,fj)=c⁡(f)=μ¯​(f)+r−1,\sum_{i=1}^{r}\overline{\mu}(f_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}c(f_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})=c(f)=\overline{\mu}(f)+r-1,

by [3, Lemma 2.1, p. 381]. Property (i​i​i)(iii) in the case r=1r=1 reduces to the Dedekind formula i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=c⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=c(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1 provided that i0​(f,l)≢0i_{0}(f,l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) [7, Lemma 3.1]. To check the general case we apply the Dedekind formula to the irreducible factors fif_{i} of ff and we get

i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))\displaystyle i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f)) =\displaystyle= ∑i=1ri0​(fi,𝒫l​(f))=∑i=1ri0​(fi,𝒫l​(fi)​ffi)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{r}i_{0}(f_{i},{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\sum_{i=1}^{r}i_{0}\left(f_{i},{\cal P}_{l}(f_{i})\frac{f}{f_{i}}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑i=1r(i0​(fi,𝒫l​(fi))+∑j≠ii0​(fi,fj))\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left(i_{0}(f_{i},{\cal P}_{l}(f_{i}))+\sum_{j\neq i}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑i=1r(μ¯​(fi)+i0​(fi,l)−1+∑j≠ii0​(fi,fj))\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left(\overline{\mu}(f_{i})+i_{0}(f_{i},l)-1+\sum_{j\neq i}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑i=1rμ¯​(fi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤ri0​(fi,fj)+i0​(f,l)−r\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{r}\overline{\mu}(f_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})+i_{0}(f,l)-r
=\displaystyle= μ¯​(f)+r−1+i0​(f,l)−r=μ¯​(f)+i0​(f,l)−1.\displaystyle\overline{\mu}(f)+r-1+i_{0}(f,l)-r=\overline{\mu}(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.

Property (i​v)(iv) follows since c⁡(f)=2​δ​(f)c(f)=2\delta(f) for any reduced power series ff by the Gorenstein theorem (see for example [20, Section 5]).

Now we prove Property (v)(v). If ff is irreducible then μ¯​(f)=c​(f)≥0\overline{\mu}(f)=c(f)\geq 0 with equality if and only if ord​(f)=1\mbox{\rm ord}(f)=1. Suppose that r>1r>1. Then by (i​i)(ii) we get

μ¯​(f)+r−1≥2​∑1≤i<j≤ri0​(fi,fj)≥r⁡(r−1)\overline{\mu}(f)+r-1\geq 2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq r}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})\geq r(r-1)

and μ¯​(f)≥(r−1)2>0\overline{\mu}(f)\geq(r-1)^{2}>0, which proves (v)(v).  

Remark 1.2

Using Proposition 1.1 (ii) we check the following property:
Let f=g1⋯gs∈𝐊[[x,y]]f=g_{1}\cdots g_{s}\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series, where the power series gig_{i} for i=1,…,si=1,\ldots,s are pairwise coprime. Then

μ¯​(f)+s−1=∑i=1sμ¯​(gi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤si0​(gi,gj).\overline{\mu}(f)+s-1=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\overline{\mu}(g_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq s}i_{0}(g_{i},g_{j}).

Let w→=(n,m)∈(𝐍+)2\overrightarrow{w}=(n,m)\in(\mathbf{N}_{+})^{2} be a pair of strictly positive integers. In the sequel we call w→\overrightarrow{w} a weight.

Let f=∑cα​β​xα​yβ∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f=\sum c_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a power series. Then

  • •

    the w→\overrightarrow{w} -order of ff is ordw→​(f)=inf{α​n+β​m:cα​β≠0}\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=\inf\{\alpha n+\beta m\;:\;c_{\alpha\beta}\neq 0\},

  • •

    the w→\overrightarrow{w}-initial form of ff is inw→​(f)=∑α​n+β​m=wcα​β​xα​yβ,\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=\sum_{\alpha n+\beta m=w}c_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}, where w=ordw→​(f)w=\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f),

  • •

    Rw→​(f)=f−inw→​(f)R_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=f-\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f).

Thus Rw→​(f)R_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) is a power series of w→\overrightarrow{w}-order greater than ordw→​(f)\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f).
Note that ordw→​(x)=n\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(x)=n and ordw→​(y)=m\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(y)=m.

A power series ff is semi-quasihomogeneous (with respect to w→\overrightarrow{w}) if the system of equations

{∂∂x​inw→​(f)=0,∂∂y​inw→​(f)=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=0,\\ \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=0\end{array}\right.

has the only solution (x,y)=(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0).

A power series ff is convenient if f⁡(x,0)⋅f⁡(0,y)≠0f(x,0)\cdot f(0,y)\neq 0.

Suppose that inw→​(f)\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) is convenient and the line α​n+β​m=ordw→​(f)\alpha n+\beta m=\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) intersects the axes in points (m,0)(m,0) and (0,n)(0,n). Let d=gcd⁡(m,n)d=\gcd(m,n). Then inw→​(f)=F⁡(xm/d,yn/d),\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=F(x^{m/d},y^{n/d}), where F⁡(u,v)∈𝐊⁡[u,v]F(u,v)\in\mathbf{K}[u,v] is a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd.

Proposition 1.3

Suppose that inw→​(f)\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) has no multiple factors. Then

μ¯​(f)=(ordw→​(f)n−1)⋅(ordw→​(f)m−1).\overline{\mu}(f)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\cdot\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right).

Proof. In the proof we will use lemmas collected in the Appendix.
Observe that if inw→​(f)\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) has no multiple factors then inw→​(f)=mw→​(f)​(inw→​(f))o\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=m_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o}, where mw→​(f)∈{1,x,y,x​y}m_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\in\{1,x,y,xy\} and (inw→​(f))o\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o} is a convenient power series or a constant. To prove the proposition we will use Hensel’s Lemma (see Lemma 5.3) and Remark 1.2. We have to consider several cases.

Case 1: inw→​(f)=(const)⋅x\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=(\hbox{\rm const})\cdot x or inw→​(f)=(const)⋅y\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=(\hbox{\rm const})\cdot y.

In this case ord​(f)=1\mbox{\rm ord}(f)=1 and by Proposition 1.1(v) μ¯​(f)=0\overline{\mu}(f)=0. If inw→​(f)=(const)⋅x\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=(\hbox{\rm const})\cdot x (resp. inw→​(f)=(const)⋅y\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=(\hbox{\rm const})\cdot y) then ordw→​(f)=n\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=n (resp. ordw→​(f)=m\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=m) and

(ordw→​(f)n−1)​(ordw→​(f)m−1)=0.\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right)=0.

Case 2: inw→​(f)=(const)⋅x​y.\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=(\hbox{\rm const})\cdot xy.

By Hensel’s Lemma (see Lemma 5.3) f=f1​f2f=f_{1}f_{2}, where inw→​(f1)=c1​x\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f_{1})=c_{1}x, inw→​(f2)=c2​y\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f_{2})=c_{2}y with constants c1,c2≠0c_{1},c_{2}\neq 0. Using Remark 1.2 and Lemma 5.1 we get

μ¯​(f)+1=μ¯​(f1​f2)+1=μ¯​(f1)+μ¯​(f2)+2​i0​(f1,f2)=0+0+2.1\overline{\mu}(f)+1=\overline{\mu}(f_{1}f_{2})+1=\overline{\mu}(f_{1})+\overline{\mu}(f_{2})+2i_{0}(f_{1},f_{2})=0+0+2.1

and μ¯​(f)=1\overline{\mu}(f)=1. On the other hand ordw→​(f)=n+m\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=n+m and

(ordw→​(f)n−1)​(ordw→​(f)m−1)=1.\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right)=1.

Case 3: The power series inw→​f\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f is convenient.

Assume additionally that the line n​α+m​β=ordw→​(f)n\alpha+m\beta=\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) intersects the axes in points (m,0)(m,0) and (0,n)(0,n). Let d=gcd⁡(n,m)d=\gcd(n,m). Then the w→\overrightarrow{w}-initial form of ff is

inw→​f=∏i=1d(ai​xm/d+bi​yn/d),\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\left(a_{i}x^{m/d}+b_{i}y^{n/d}\right),

where ai​xm/d+bi​yn/da_{i}x^{m/d}+b_{i}y^{n/d} are pairwise coprime. By Hensel’s Lemma (see Lemma 5.3) we get a factorization f=∏i=1dfif=\prod_{i=1}^{d}f_{i}, where inw→​fi=ai​xm/d+bi​yn/d\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f_{i}=a_{i}x^{m/d}+b_{i}y^{n/d} for i=1,…,di=1,\ldots,d. The factors fif_{i} are irreducible with semigroup Γ⁡(fi)=md​𝐍+nd​𝐍\Gamma(f_{i})=\frac{m}{d}\mathbf{N}+\frac{n}{d}\mathbf{N} and

μ¯​(fi)=c⁡(fi)=(md−1)​(nd−1)\overline{\mu}(f_{i})=c(f_{i})=\left(\frac{m}{d}-1\right)\left(\frac{n}{d}-1\right)

(see, for example [6]). Moreover by Lemma 5.1 we have

i0​(fi,fj)=ordw→​fi​ordw→​fjm​n=m​nd2,for ​i≠ji_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})=\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f_{i}\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f_{j}}{mn}=\frac{mn}{d^{2}},\;\hbox{\rm for }i\neq j

and we get by Proposition 1.1(ii)

μ¯​(f)+d−1=∑i=1dμ¯​(fi)+2​∑1≤i<j≤di0​(fi,fj)=d⁡(md−1)​(nd−1)+2​d⁡(d−1)2​m​nd2,\overline{\mu}(f)+d-1=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\overline{\mu}(f_{i})+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq d}i_{0}(f_{i},f_{j})=d\left(\frac{m}{d}-1\right)\left(\frac{n}{d}-1\right)+2\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\frac{mn}{d^{2}},

which implies μ¯​(f)=(m−1)​(n−1)=(ordw→​fn−1)​(ordw→​fm−1)\overline{\mu}(f)=(m-1)(n-1)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f}{m}-1\right), since the weighted order of ff is ordw→​f=m​n\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f=mn.

Now consider the general case, that is when the line n​α+m​β=ordw→​(f)n\alpha+m\beta=\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) intersects the axes in points (m1,0)=(ordw→​fn,0)(m_{1},0)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}f}{n},0\right) and (0,n1)=(0,ordw→​(f)m)(0,n_{1})=\left(0,\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}\right). Then ff is semi-quasihomogeneous with respect to w1→=(n1,m1)\overrightarrow{w_{1}}=(n_{1},m_{1}) and the line n1​α+m1​β=ordw1→​(f)n_{1}\alpha+m_{1}\beta=\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w_{1}}}(f) intersects the axes in points (m1,0)(m_{1},0) and (0,n1)(0,n_{1}). By the first part of the proof we get

μ¯​(f)=(m1−1)​(n1−1)=(ordw→​(f)n−1)​(ordw→​(f)m−1),\overline{\mu}(f)=(m_{1}-1)(n_{1}-1)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right),

which proves the proposition in Case 3.

Case 4: inw→​(f)=x​(inw→​(f))o\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=x\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o} or inw→​(f)=y​(inw→​(f))o\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=y\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o}, where (inw→​(f))o\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o} is convenient.

This case follows from Hensel’s Lemma (Lemma 5.3), Case 1 and Case 3.

Case 5: inw→​(f)=x​y​(inw→​(f))o\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=xy\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o}, where (inw→​(f))o\left(\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)\right)^{o} is convenient.

This case follows from Hensel’s Lemma (Lemma 5.3), Case 2 and Case 3.
 

Theorem 1.4

Suppose that inw→​(f)\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f) has no multiple factors. Then ff is tame if and only if ff is a semi-quasihomogeneous singularity with respect to w→\overrightarrow{w}.

Proof. We have μ¯​(f)=(ordw→​(f)n−1)​(ordw→​(f)m−1)\overline{\mu}(f)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right) by Proposition 1.3. On the other hand, by Lemma 5.2, we get that μ⁡(f)=(ordw→​(f)n−1)​(ordw→​(f)m−1){\mu}(f)=\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{n}-1\right)\left(\frac{\mbox{\rm ord}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)}{m}-1\right) if and only if the system of equations

{∂∂x​inw→​(f)=0,∂∂y​inw→​(f)=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=0,\\ \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=0\end{array}\right.

has the only solution (x,y)=(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0). The theorem follows from Proposition 1.1(iv).  

Example 1.5

Let f⁡(x,y)=xm+yn+∑α​n+β​m>n​mcα​β​xα​yβf(x,y)=x^{m}+y^{n}+\sum_{\alpha n+\beta m>nm}c_{\alpha\,\beta}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta} and let d=gcd⁡(m,n)d=\gcd(m,n). Then inw→​(f)=xm+yn\mbox{\rm in}_{\overrightarrow{w}}(f)=x^{m}+y^{n} has no multiple factors if and only if d≢0d\not\equiv 0 (mod pp). If d≢0d\not\equiv 0 (mod pp) then ff is tame if and only if m≢0m\not\equiv 0 (mod pp) and n≢0n\not\equiv 0 (mod pp).

Corollary 1.6

The semi-quasihomogeneous singularities are tame.

Corollary 1.6 is a particular case of the following

Theorem 1.7

(Boubakri, Greuel, Markwig [1, Theorem 9]). The planar Newton non-degenerate singularities are tame.

2 Teissier’s lemma in characteristic p≥0p\geq 0

The intersection theoretical approach to the Milnor number in characteristic zero [4] is based on a lemma due to Teissier who proved a more general result (the case of hypersurfaces) in [22, Chapter II, Proposition 1.2]. A general formula on isolated complete intersection singularity is due to Greuel [8] and Lê [14]. In this section we study Teissier’s Lemma in arbitrary characteristic p≥0p\geq 0.

Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series and l∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]l\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a regular parameter. Assume that ll does not divide ff and consider the polar 𝒫l​(f)=∂f∂x​∂l∂y−∂f∂y​∂l∂x{\cal P}_{l}(f)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial l}{\partial x} of ff with respect to ll. In this section we assume, without loss of generality, that ord​(l​(0,y))=1\mbox{\rm ord}(l(0,y))=1.

Lemma 2.1

Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series and l∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]l\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a regular parameter. Then i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))≥i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}\left(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f)\right)\geq i_{0}(f,l)-1 with equality if and only if i0​(f,l)≢0i_{0}(f,l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).

Proof. Recall that ord​(l​(0,y))=1\mbox{\rm ord}(l(0,y))=1. Let ϕ⁡(t)=(ϕ1​(t),ϕ2​(t))\phi(t)=(\phi_{1}(t),\phi_{2}(t)) be a good parametrization of the curve l⁡(x,y)=0l(x,y)=0 (see [19, Section 2]. In particular 0=l⁡(ϕ⁡(t))0=l(\phi(t)) so dd​t​l​(ϕ⁡(t))=0\frac{d}{dt}l(\phi(t))=0. On the other hand we have ord​(ϕ1​(t))=i0​(x,l)=ord​(l⁡(0,y))=1\mbox{\rm ord}(\phi_{1}(t))=i_{0}(x,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(l(0,y))=1 and ϕ1′​(0)≠0\phi^{\prime}_{1}(0)\neq 0. Differentiating f⁡(ϕ⁡(t))f(\phi(t)) and l⁡(ϕ⁡(t))l(\phi(t)) we get

dd​t​f​(ϕ⁡(t))=∂f∂x​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ1′​(t)+∂f∂y​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ2′​(t)\frac{d}{dt}f(\phi(t))=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{1}(t)+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{2}(t)\\ (1)

and

0=dd​t​l​(ϕ⁡(t))=∂l∂x​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ1′​(t)+∂l∂y​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ2′​(t).0=\frac{d}{dt}l(\phi(t))=\frac{\partial l}{\partial x}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{1}(t)+\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{2}(t).\\ (2)

From (2) we have ∂l∂x​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ1′​(t)=−∂l∂y​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ2′​(t)\frac{\partial l}{\partial x}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{1}(t)=-\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{2}(t) and by (1) and the definition of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get

𝒫l​(f)​(ϕ⁡(t))​ϕ1′​(t)=dd​t​f​(ϕ⁡(t))​∂l∂y​(ϕ⁡(t)).{\cal P}_{l}(f)(\phi(t))\phi^{\prime}_{1}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}f(\phi(t))\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\phi(t)).

Since ϕ1′​(t)\phi^{\prime}_{1}(t) and ∂l∂y​(ϕ​(t))\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\phi(t)) are units in 𝐊⁡[[t]]\mathbf{K}[[t]] we have

ord​(𝒫l​(f)​(ϕ⁡(t)))=ord​(dd​t​f​(ϕ⁡(t)))≥ord​(f⁡(ϕ⁡(t)))−1,\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f)(\phi(t)))=\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{d}{dt}f(\phi(t))\right)\geq\mbox{\rm ord}(f(\phi(t)))-1,

with equality if and only if ord​(f​(ϕ​(t)))≢0\mbox{\rm ord}(f(\phi(t)))\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p). Now the lemma follows from the formula i0​(h,l)=ord​(h⁡(ϕ⁡(t)))i_{0}(h,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(h(\phi(t))) which holds for every power series h∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]h\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]].  

Corollary 2.2

Suppose that i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)≢0i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) for a regular parameter l∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]l\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]]. Then

  1. (a)

    i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))=ord​(f)−1i_{0}(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1,

  2. (b)

    ord​(𝒫l​(f))=ord​(f)−1\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1,

  3. (c)

    if hh is an irreducible factor of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) then i0​(l,h)=ord​(h)i_{0}(l,h)=\mbox{\rm ord}(h).

Proof. Property (a)(a) follows immediately from Lemma 2.1. To check (b)(b) observe that we get ord​(𝒫l​(f))=ord​(𝒫l​(f))⋅ord​(l)≤i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))=ord​(f)−1\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))\cdot\mbox{\rm ord}(l)\leq i_{0}(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1, where the last equality follows from (a)(a). The inequality ord​(𝒫l​(f))≥ord​(f)−1\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))\geq\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1 is obvious.

Let 𝒫l​(f)=∏i=1shi{\cal P}_{l}(f)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}h_{i}, where hih_{i} is irreducible. From (a)(a) and (b)(b) we get

0=i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))−ord​(𝒫l​(f))=∑i=1s(i0​(l,hi)−ord​(hi)).0=i_{0}(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f))-\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\left(i_{0}(l,h_{i})-\mbox{\rm ord}(h_{i})\right).

Since i0​(l,hi)≥ord​(hi)i_{0}(l,h_{i})\geq\mbox{\rm ord}(h_{i}) we have i0​(l,hi)=ord​(hi)i_{0}(l,h_{i})=\mbox{\rm ord}(h_{i}) for i=1,…,si=1,\ldots,s which proves (c)(c).  

Proposition 2.3

(Teissier’s Lemma in characteristic pp). Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series. Suppose that

  1. (i)

    i0​(f,l)≢0i_{0}(f,l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p),

  2. (ii)

    for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get i0​(l,h)≢0i_{0}(l,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).

Then

i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≤μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\leq\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1

with equality if and only if

  1. (iii)

    for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).

Proof. Fix an irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) and let ψ⁡(t)=(ψ1​(t),ψ2​(t))\psi(t)=(\psi_{1}(t),\psi_{2}(t)) be a good parametrization of the curve h⁡(x,y)=0h(x,y)=0. Then ord​(l⁡(ψ⁡(t)))=i0​(l,h)≢0\mbox{\rm ord}(l(\psi(t)))=i_{0}(l,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) by (i​i)(ii) and ord​(dd​t​l​(ψ⁡(t)))=ord​(l⁡(ψ⁡(t)))−1\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{d}{dt}l(\psi(t))\right)=\mbox{\rm ord}(l(\psi(t)))-1. Differentiating f⁡(ψ⁡(t))f(\psi(t)) and l⁡(ψ⁡(t))l(\psi(t)) we get

dd​t​f​(ψ⁡(t))=∂f∂x​(ψ⁡(t))​ψ1′​(t)+∂f∂y​(ψ⁡(t))​ψ2′​(t),\frac{d}{dt}f(\psi(t))=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(\psi(t))\psi^{\prime}_{1}(t)+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\psi(t))\psi^{\prime}_{2}(t), (3)

and

dd​t​l​(ψ⁡(t))=∂l∂x​(ψ⁡(t))​ψ1′​(t)+∂l∂y​(ψ⁡(t))​ψ2′​(t).\frac{d}{dt}l(\psi(t))=\frac{\partial l}{\partial x}(\psi(t))\psi^{\prime}_{1}(t)+\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\psi(t))\psi^{\prime}_{2}(t). (4)

Since 𝒫l​(f)​(ψ⁡(t))=0{\cal P}_{l}(f)(\psi(t))=0, it follows from (3) and (4) that

dd​t​f​(ψ⁡(t))​∂l∂y​(ψ⁡(t))=dd​t​l​(ψ⁡(t))​∂f∂y​(ψ⁡(t)).\frac{d}{dt}f(\psi(t))\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\psi(t))=\frac{d}{dt}l(\psi(t))\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\psi(t)). (5)

Since ∂l∂y​(ψ​(t))\frac{\partial l}{\partial y}(\psi(t)) is a unit in 𝐊⁡[[t]]\mathbf{K}[[t]], taking orders in (5) we have

ord​(f​(ψ​(t)))−1\displaystyle\mbox{\rm ord}(f(\psi(t)))-1 ≤\displaystyle\leq ord​(dd​t​f​(ψ⁡(t)))=ord​(dd​t​l​(ψ⁡(t)))+ord​(∂f∂y​(ψ⁡(t)))\displaystyle\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{d}{dt}f(\psi(t))\right)=\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{d}{dt}l(\psi(t))\right)+\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\psi(t))\right)
=\displaystyle= ord​(l⁡(ψ⁡(t)))−1+ord​(∂f∂y​(ψ⁡(t))),\displaystyle\mbox{\rm ord}(l(\psi(t)))-1+\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\psi(t))\right),

where the last equality follows from ord​(l​(ψ​(t)))≢0\mbox{\rm ord}(l(\psi(t)))\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).
Hence i0​(f,h)≤i0​(l,h)+i0​(∂f∂y,h).i_{0}(f,h)\leq i_{0}(l,h)+i_{0}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},h\right).

Summing up over all hh counted with multiplicities as factors of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we obtain

i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≤i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))+i0​(∂f∂y,𝒫l​(f)).i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\leq i_{0}(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f))+i_{0}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},{\cal P}_{l}(f)\right). (6)

By Lemma 2.1 and assumption (i)(i) we have i0​(l,𝒫l​(f))=i0​(f,l)−1.i_{0}\left(l,{\cal P}_{l}(f)\right)=i_{0}(f,l)-1. Moreover i0​(∂f∂y,𝒫l​(f))=μ⁡(f)i_{0}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},{\cal P}_{l}(f)\right)=\mu(f) since ord​(l​(0,y))=1\mbox{\rm ord}(l(0,y))=1 and we get from the equality (6)

i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≤μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1.i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\leq\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.

The equality holds if and only if i0​(f,h)=i0​(l,h)+i0​(∂f∂y,h)i_{0}(f,h)=i_{0}(l,h)+i_{0}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},h\right) for every hh, which is equivalent to the condition i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p), since i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) if and only if ord​(dd​t​f​(ψ⁡(t)))=ord​(f⁡(ψ⁡(t)))−1\mbox{\rm ord}\left(\frac{d}{dt}f(\psi(t))\right)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f(\psi(t)))-1.  

Corollary 2.4

(Teissier [22, Chapter II, Proposition 1.2]). If char​𝐊=0\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}=0 then

i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1.i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.
Corollary 2.5

Suppose that p=char​𝐊>ord​(f)p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}>\mbox{\rm ord}(f) and let i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f). Then

i0​(𝒫l​(f),f)≤μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1.i_{0}({\cal P}_{l}(f),f)\leq\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.

The equality holds if and only if for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).

Proof. If ord​(f)<p\mbox{\rm ord}(f)<p then i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)≢0i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) and by Corollary 2.2 for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get

i0​(l,h)=ord​(h)≤ord​(𝒫l​(f))=ord​(f)−1<p.i_{0}(l,h)=\mbox{\rm ord}(h)\leq\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1<p.

Hence i0​(l,h)≢0i_{0}(l,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) and the corollary follows from Proposition 2.3.  

Example 2.6

Let f=xp+2+yp+1+xp+1​yf=x^{p+2}+y^{p+1}+x^{p+1}y, where p=char​K>2p=\mathrm{char}\,K>2. Take l=yl=y. Then i0​(f,l)=p+2≢0i_{0}(f,l)=p+2\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p), 𝒫l​(f)=∂f∂x=xp​(2​x+y){\cal P}_{l}(f)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=x^{p}(2x+y) and the irreducible factors of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) are h1=xh_{1}=x and h2=2​x+yh_{2}=2x+y. Clearly i0​(l,h1)=i0​(l,h2)=1≢0i_{0}(l,h_{1})=i_{0}(l,h_{2})=1\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p). Moreover i0​(f,h1)=i0​(f,h2)=p+1i_{0}(f,h_{1})=i_{0}(f,h_{2})=p+1 and all assumptions of Proposition 2.3 are satisfied.

Hence i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1 and μ⁡(f)=i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))−i0​(f,l)+1=p⁡(p+1)\mu(f)=i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))-i_{0}(f,l)+1=p(p+1). Note that l=0l=0 is a curve of maximal contact with f=0f=0. Let l1=xl_{1}=x. Then i0​(f,l1)=ord​(f)=p+1i_{0}(f,l_{1})=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)=p+1, 𝒫l1​(f)=−(yp+xp+1){\cal P}_{l_{1}}(f)=-(y^{p}+x^{p+1}) and h=yp+xp+1h=y^{p}+x^{p+1} is the only irreducible factor of the polar 𝒫l1​(f){\cal P}_{l_{1}}(f). Since i0​(l1,h)=pi_{0}(l_{1},h)=p, the condition (i​i)(ii) of Proposition 2.3 is not satisfied. However, i0​(f,𝒫l1​(f))=μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l1)−1,i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l_{1}}(f))=\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l_{1})-1, which we check directly.

3 Tame singularities

Assume that ff is a plane curve singularity.

Proposition 3.1

Let f=f1⋯fr∈𝐊[[x,y]]f=f_{1}\cdots f_{r}\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be a reduced power series, where fif_{i} is irreducible for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Suppose that there exists a regular parameter ll such that i0​(fi,l)≢0i_{0}(f_{i},l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Then ff is tame if and only if Teissier’s lemma holds, that is if i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1.

Proof. By Proposition 1.1 (i​i​i)(iii) we have that i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ¯​(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\overline{\mu}(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1. Thus i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))=μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))=\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1 if and only if μ​(f)=μ¯​(f)\mu(f)=\overline{\mu}(f). We finish the proof using Proposition 1.1 (i​v)(iv).  

Proposition 3.2

(Milnor [17], Risler [21]). If char​𝐊=0\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}=0 then any plane singularity is tame.

Proof. Teissier’s Lemma holds by Corollary 2.4 . Use Proposition 3.1.  

Proposition 3.3

Let p=char​𝐊>0p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}>0. Suppose that p>ord​(f)p>\mbox{\rm ord}(f). Let ll be a regular parameter such that i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f). Then ff is tame if and only if for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we get i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p).

Proof. Take a regular parameter ll such that i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f). By hypothesis we get i0​(f,l)<pi_{0}(f,l)<p so i0​(f,l)≢0i_{0}(f,l)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p). By Corollary 2.2 the assumption (i​i)(ii) of Proposition 2.3 is satisfied.

Hence i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≤μ⁡(f)+i0​(f,l)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\leq\mu(f)+i_{0}(f,l)-1 with equality if and only if i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f). Use Proposition 3.1.  

Proposition 3.4

(Nguyen [18]). Let p=char​𝐊>0p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}>0. Suppose that there exists a regular parameter ll such that i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f) and i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))<pi_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))<p. Then ff is tame.

Proof. We have p>i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≥ord​(f)⋅ord​(𝒫l​(f))p>i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\geq\mbox{\rm ord}(f)\cdot\mbox{\rm ord}({\cal P}_{l}(f)). Hence p>ord​(f)p>\mbox{\rm ord}(f) and we may apply Proposition 3.3. Since i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))<pi_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))<p for any irreducible factor hh of 𝒫l​(f){\cal P}_{l}(f) we have that i0​(f,h)<pi_{0}(f,h)<p and obviously i0​(f,h)≢0i_{0}(f,h)\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p). The proposition follows from Proposition 3.3.  

Theorem 3.5

(Nguyen [18]). If p>μ​(f)+ord​(f)−1p>\mu(f)+\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1 then ff is tame.

Proof. Since ff is a singularity we get μ⁡(f)>0\mu(f)>0 and by hypothesis the characteristic of the field verifies p>μ⁡(f)−1+ord​(f)≥ord​(f)p>\mu(f)-1+\mbox{\rm ord}(f)\geq\mbox{\rm ord}(f). By the first part of the proof of Proposition 3.3 we have i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))≤μ⁡(f)+ord​(f)−1i_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))\leq\mu(f)+\mbox{\rm ord}(f)-1, where ll is a regular parameter such that i0​(f,l)=ord​(f)i_{0}(f,l)=\mbox{\rm ord}(f). Hence i0​(f,𝒫l​(f))<pi_{0}(f,{\cal P}_{l}(f))<p and the theorem follows from Proposition 3.4.  

4 The Milnor number of plane irreducible singularities

Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be an irreducible power series of order n=ord​(f)n=\mbox{\rm ord}(f) and let Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) be the semigroup associated with f=0f=0.

Let β0¯,…,βg¯\overline{\beta_{0}},\ldots,\overline{\beta_{g}} be the minimal sequence of generators of Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) defined by the conditions

  • •

    β0¯=min⁡(Γ⁡(f)\{0})=ord​(f)=n\overline{\beta_{0}}=\min(\Gamma(f)\backslash\{0\})=\mbox{\rm ord}(f)=n,

  • •

    βk¯=min⁡(Γ⁡(f)\𝐍​β0¯+⋯+𝐍​βk−1¯)\overline{\beta_{k}}=\min(\Gamma(f)\backslash\mathbf{N}\overline{\beta_{0}}+\cdots+\mathbf{N}\overline{\beta_{k-1}}) for k∈{1,…,g},k\in\{1,\ldots,g\},

  • •

    Γ⁡(f)=𝐍​β0¯+⋯+𝐍​βg¯\Gamma(f)=\mathbf{N}\overline{\beta_{0}}+\cdots+\mathbf{N}\overline{\beta_{g}}.

Let ek=gcd⁡(β0¯,…,βk¯)e_{k}=\gcd(\overline{\beta_{0}},\ldots,\overline{\beta_{k}}) for k∈{1,…,g}.k\in\{1,\ldots,g\}. Then n=e0>e1>⋯eg−1>eg=1n=e_{0}>e_{1}>\cdots e_{g-1}>e_{g}=1. Let nk=ek−1/ekn_{k}=e_{k-1}/e_{k} for k∈{1,…,g}.k\in\{1,\ldots,g\}. We have nk>1n_{k}>1 for k∈{1,…,g}k\in\{1,\ldots,g\} and n=n1⋯ngn=n_{1}\cdots n_{g}. Let n∗=max⁡(n1,…,ng)n^{*}=\max(n_{1},\ldots,n_{g}). Then n∗≤nn^{*}\leq n with equality if and only if g=1g=1.

The following theorem is a sharpened version of the main result of [7].

Theorem 4.1

Let f∈𝐊⁡[[x,y]]f\in\mathbf{K}[[x,y]] be an irreducible power series of order n>1n>1 and let β0¯,…,βg¯\overline{\beta_{0}},\ldots,\overline{\beta_{g}} be the minimal system of generators of Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f). Suppose that p=char​𝐊>n∗p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}>n^{*}. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:

In [11] the authors proved, without any restriction on p=char​𝐊p=\mathrm{char}\,\mathbf{K}, the following profound result:

Theorem 4.6

(Hefez, Rodrigues, Salomão [11], [12]). Let Γ⁡(f)=β0¯​𝐍+⋯+βg¯​𝐍\Gamma(f)=\overline{\beta_{0}}\mathbf{N}+\cdots+\overline{\beta_{g}}\mathbf{N}. If β¯k≢0\overline{\beta}_{k}\not\equiv 0 (mod​p\mathrm{mod}\,p) for k=0,…,gk=0,\ldots,g then ff is tame.

The question as to whether the converse of Theorem 4.6 is true remains open.
